client: I've been feeling really lost ever since my grandmother passed away last month. It's like this heavy sadness just sits on my chest all the time, and I keep finding myself questioning what any of it even means for my own life going forward. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for giving this a try, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that kind of courage matters. Losing your grandmother and then facing those bigger questions about meaning and your own path forward sounds like an incredibly heavy weight to carry. I'd really like to sit with you in this and gently explore what's been coming up for you — can you tell me a little more about what "lost" feels like for you day to day?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, "lost" feels like... I wake up in the morning and I just don't really know why I'm doing any of it. Like, I go through the motions — work, eating, whatever — but there's this hollow feeling underneath everything, like I'm just waiting for something but I don't even know what. My grandmother was kind of my anchor, and now that she's gone, I keep asking myself what any of this is actually for, and I don't have an answer.
therapist: That image of your grandmother as your anchor is so powerful — it makes a lot of sense that without her, everything feels unmoored and the "why" behind daily life has gone quiet. That hollow, going-through-the-motions feeling is a really common part of grief, especially when someone was so central to your sense of meaning and direction. I'm curious — when you think back to what your grandmother meant to you, what is it about her presence that made things feel like they had purpose?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: She just had this way of making me feel like I mattered, like whatever I was doing or going through actually meant something to someone. Even when I was just telling her about something small, like a book I read or a frustrating day at work, she listened like it was the most important thing in the world. I think that's what's gone now — there's no one who holds that space for me anymore, and I didn't realize how much I depended on that to feel real, I guess.
therapist: What you just described — being truly *seen* by someone — is one of the most profound human needs, and she clearly gave you that in a way that felt effortless and unconditional. I notice as you were sharing that, your words carried something tender but also something that sounded almost urgent, like this realization is still a little raw and surprising even to you. I'm wondering — does it feel strange or even a little vulnerable to recognize just how much of your sense of "being real" was held by her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, it does feel strange, honestly. Like I didn't fully realize how much I was relying on her to feel like a real, worthwhile person until she was gone, and now that I see it, it's almost embarrassing. I don't know if that says something broken about me, or if it's just... what happens when you lose someone who really knew you.
therapist: There's nothing broken about you — what you're describing is actually a sign of how deeply and healthily you could attach to someone, and that's a gift, not a flaw. I notice there's something in the way you're talking about this that feels a little rushed, like maybe part of you wants to move past the vulnerability of that realization before it fully lands. What comes up for you when you sit with the idea that needing to feel seen and valued by someone you loved isn't a weakness — it's just being human?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... I hear what you're saying, but it's hard to just sit with that without immediately wanting to argue against it. Like, part of me is already thinking "okay but if it's so normal and healthy, why did it still push him away?" I guess I do rush past it because if I actually let myself believe I wasn't wrong for wanting to feel loved, then I have to face how much it hurt that it still wasn't enough.
therapist: That last part you said — "it still wasn't enough" — that feels like it carries a lot, and I want to make sure we don't rush past it either. It sounds like there might be a painful story underneath this grief about your grandmother, one where wanting to be loved and seen also got tangled up with feeling like you somehow failed or fell short with someone else. Can you tell me a little more about who you mean when you say "him"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah... "him" is my dad. I guess I've been avoiding saying it out loud because once I do, it feels like I'm making this whole thing about him when it's supposed to be about my grandmother, and that feels disloyal to her somehow. But the truth is, she was the one person who made me feel like I was enough, and when she died, I lost that — and I realized I'd never really had it from him, no matter how hard I tried.
therapist: What you just said took real courage, and I want you to know that naming your dad doesn't betray your grandmother at all — if anything, it honors her, because she was clearly the one who held what he couldn't give you. There's something very quiet in the way you're carrying this, like you've been holding it carefully for a long time, almost like you're afraid of how much weight it actually has. I'm gently wondering — what has it been like, all these years, to keep trying with him while she was the one who kept catching you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It's exhausting, honestly. Like I've been running toward a door that never opens, and every time I'd fall, my grandmother would just... be there, quietly picking me up without making a big deal of it. And now that she's gone, I think part of what scares me is that I don't have that safety net anymore, so trying with him feels even riskier than it used to.
therapist: That image of running toward a door that never opens is exhausting just to hear, and you've been living it — so of course losing her feels like losing the ground beneath your feet, not just a person. What strikes me is that even as you describe something so draining, there's an energy in how you're talking about it, like part of you is still very much *in* it, still feeling the pull toward that door. I'm curious — when you imagine what it would mean to stop running toward him, does that feel like relief, or does it feel like losing something too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: It feels like losing something, honestly — even though I know that sounds irrational. Like if I stop reaching for that door, I'm admitting it was never going to open, and then what does that say about all the time and hope I poured into it? There's also this fear that if I let go, I'll just be left with this huge empty space and nothing to fill it.
therapist: It doesn't sound irrational at all — letting go of hope, even hope for something painful, is its own kind of loss, and that deserves to be grieved too. What you're describing actually makes a lot of sense in CBT terms: the time and hope you've invested can make it feel like stopping means all of it was worthless, when really it just means you were someone who loved deeply and kept trying. I want to gently offer this — what if that empty space isn't something to be feared, but something that, for the first time, you actually get to fill on your own terms?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but honestly, the idea of filling that space on my own terms just feels overwhelming right now. Like, I don't even know who I am outside of this relationship anymore — I've spent so long trying to make it work that I've kind of lost track of what I actually want. And what if I get to choose, and I still choose wrong, or end up alone anyway?
therapist: The fear of choosing wrong, or still ending up alone — that's such a vulnerable thing to say out loud, and I want you to know it makes complete sense after years of pouring yourself into something that didn't give back what you needed. I notice there's something almost quiet and careful in how you're saying this, like you're holding these fears very gently, maybe because they feel too big to look at directly. I'm wondering — when you imagine "choosing wrong," what does that actually look like to you, and whose voice is it that tells you that's what will happen?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: When I imagine choosing wrong, it looks like... being five years in with someone new and realizing I've made the same mistake, that I've ignored the same warning signs because I just wanted so badly not to be alone. And the voice — honestly, it sounds like my own, but also kind of like my mom's, because she stayed in a bad marriage for decades and I always swore I wouldn't do that, and now I wonder if I'm just wired the same way. It's like I don't fully trust my own judgment anymore, and that's the scariest part — not the loneliness itself, but the idea that I can't tell the difference between something real and something I'm just... settling for.
therapist: What you just described — that fear of becoming your mother's story — is one of the most honest and self-aware things you've shared, and it tells me your judgment is actually more intact than you're giving it credit for. The fact that you can name the pattern, trace where it comes from, and feel the difference between real connection and settling shows a kind of clarity that someone "wired wrong" simply wouldn't have. I'm curious — what do you think it would feel like, in your body or your gut, if something *was* real rather than just filling the empty space?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
